title: Do You Work in a Take Credit or Share Credit Culture
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article draws a distinction between organizations where openly touting individual wins is expected, and organizations where crediting colleagues and downplaying personal contribution is the unspoken norm. It notes that while the best leaders themselves often deflect credit, the rules for team members vary widely by workplace culture, and misreading which culture you're in can quietly damage how you're perceived. The author warns that colleagues rarely explain the norm directly; instead they simply conclude a newcomer doesn't fit. The piece suggests watching how the most tenured, respected people self-promote as the best clue to the unwritten rule.
points: Take Credit cultures expect people to openly tout their wins; Share Credit cultures expect deflection to colleagues
Leaders often deflect credit themselves even in Take Credit cultures, but the norm for team members varies
Violating the unwritten credit-sharing norm is rarely explained directly; people just quietly conclude you don't fit
Watch how the most tenured, trusted colleagues talk about their wins to learn your organization's real norm
quotes: Some organizations are Take Credit workplaces, where, as long as the team member or team doesn’t go too far, it is perfectly acceptable and expected to tout good outcomes and results.
Other organizations are Share Credit workplaces, where it is considered bad form to claim individual responsibility for positive results.
Colleagues don’t always tell others they are violating the cultural norm regarding sharing or taking credit.
This can have a devastating effect on a team member’s trajectory and acceptance.
For long-term success, follow their lead. In the end, the best self-promotion matches the expectations and practices of your trusted colleagues.
